overview: The atlas's “Bashkirs” is a broad people-label, not a demonstrated ninth-century state. Its sole feature appears at 800 as one polygon across the eastern and southern Trans-Urals; Ufa, Birsk, and Sterlitamak lie outside in the atlas's Volga Bulgar area. Archaeology places Uyelgi and the wider Karayakupovo horizon near this time, but researchers describe a polyethnic landscape with Ugric-background and Turkic-associated communities. Pots, belts, horse gear, ornaments, graves, and DNA can reveal contacts and kin groups; none stamps a modern nationality onto every burial. A Bashkir mention attached to Sallam's 842-843 journey occurs only in a much later recension, while Ibn Fadlan's detailed outsider account dates to 922, after this card ends. Historical linguistics likewise warns that a homogeneous Bashkir-speaking community cannot be projected this far back. No securely datable Bashkir-language sentence survives from 800 to 900. The closest useful writing sample is the Arabic outsider name Bāshghird, explicitly labeled later and external. At 900 the software repaints the footprint as Oghuz Turks. That seam is not proof of a mass migration, a conquest on New Year's Day, or the extinction of local families.

periods.title: 800 to 815: an archaeological horizon, not a new state
periods.summary: The atlas starts its Bashkirs label at 800. Uyelgi's earliest dated complexes cluster around the turn of the ninth century, and its early group belongs mainly to this century. A cemetery horizon supplies material chronology, not a coronation date, national census, or border survey for a unified Bashkir realm.

periods.title: 815 to 830: contacts cross the Southern Urals
periods.summary: Uyelgi combines Southern Ural nomadic burial practice with objects related to Srostki, Altai, and Ugric-associated traditions. Archaeologists identify several cultural horizons rather than one sealed population. The teaching slice marks continuing interaction; no source reports a political event exactly at either boundary.

periods.title: 830 to 842: sparse names, complicated material lives
periods.summary: Kushnarenkovo and related finds mix mobile-steppe and forest-steppe features, while many excavated graves were disturbed before modern study. Researchers can reconstruct objects and connections more securely than the names people used for themselves. This interval is intentionally quiet because the evidence does not justify invented rulers.

periods.title: 842 to 847: Sallam's journey and a textual trap
periods.summary: Sallam al-Tarjuman traveled east in 842-843, but Ibn Khordadbeh's earlier recension does not name Bashkirs. The Bashkir country appears in al-Idrisi's twelfth-century version. The later wording may preserve older information, yet it cannot serve as an uncontested contemporary attestation for this exact interval.

periods.title: 847 to 870: geographic labels remain uncertain
periods.summary: Muslim geographic traditions were copied, combined, and revised, sometimes using Bashghird for populations identified elsewhere with Magyars. Routes and ethnonyms therefore require source-by-source criticism. The absence of a secure local archive means this period cannot honestly be filled with a royal sequence or fixed tribal map.

periods.title: 870 to 893: exchange reaches across the Volga-Ural world
periods.summary: Coins moved through the Volga-Ural region as commodities and payment while Khazar-linked and later Bulgar networks changed. Finds can demonstrate circulation without identifying every carrier or buyer. The atlas polygon sat near wider exchange corridors, but a coin route is not evidence that one Bashkir government taxed all traffic.

periods.title: 893 to 898: steppe alliances shift nearby
periods.summary: UNESCO's regional synthesis places an Oghuz-Khazar defeat of Pechenegs around 893-898. A Bajgird group may have been involved, but the identification with elements of later Bashkirs is explicitly uncertain. This mobile political setting matters, while the atlas's exact polygon and one-word label remain editorial simplifications.

periods.title: 898 to 900: the card ends before the clearest account
periods.summary: No contemporary report records a state-ending event at 900. The atlas simply removes the label and paints Oghuz Turks across its eastern and southern probes. Ibn Fadlan's detailed encounter comes in 922. The endpoint is therefore a map seam placed before the strongest narrative evidence, not a dated ending.

sections.title: First read the atlas literally, then cautiously

items.text: The index contains exactly one Bashkirs record, marked circa from 800 to 900, with no finished card. Only world-800 contains its feature. The date range is precise metadata about the website, while the circa flag warns that it is not a year-by-year historical boundary record.

The decoded feature is one polygon with one ring and fifteen positions. Its bounds run from 55.604356°E to 70.382504°E and 50.759778°N to 57.578143°N. Geometry is useful for auditing what the site displays; six-decimal coordinates should not be confused with medieval surveying.

Beloretsk, Sibay, Magnitogorsk, Chelyabinsk, and Orsk test inside. Ufa, Birsk, Sterlitamak, Ishimbay, Yekaterinburg, Perm, Izhevsk, Kazan, Bolghar, Samara, Orenburg, Tobolsk, and Saranpaul test outside. Those probes make the label's eastern and southern emphasis visible and expose how little the shape resembles a modern republic.

At 800 the atlas assigns Ufa, Birsk, Sterlitamak, and Ishimbay to Volga Bulgars, not Bashkirs. That surprising separation is part of the map's own data. It prevents this card from quietly moving the polygon westward to match the borders or capital of modern Bashkortostan.

The target shares imported arcs with Paleo-Siberian Hunter-Gatherers, Volga Bulgars, Mordvinians, Permians, and Finno-Ugric Taiga Hunter-Gatherers. Shared arcs show how digital shapes touch. They do not prove that five sharply bounded peoples met at guarded checkpoints or used the website's modern labels themselves.

sections.title: A people-label is not a ready-made kingdom

items.text: No reviewed source supplies a Bashkir king, capital, law code, tax system, or unified state covering this polygon between 800 and 900. The record is safest as an ethnogeographic teaching label. Political organization may have existed at several scales, but its exact forms cannot be reconstructed from the map color.

Sallam's 842-843 journey is often introduced as the first Bashkir mention. The earlier Ibn Khordadbeh version does not contain it; the name occurs in al-Idrisi's twelfth-century retelling. A later layer might preserve earlier knowledge, but calling it a secure 843 eyewitness label would overstate the text.

Arabic and Persian geographic works sometimes use forms of Bashghird in passages connected with Magyars, and their source layers can be chronologically tangled. Similar-looking names do not automatically identify one unchanged people. Historians must ask which author, manuscript layer, route, and population each occurrence actually describes.

Historical linguistics dates the formation of Bashkir as a distinct Kipchak-type language much later and rejects a straight family-tree story from an early ethnonym to a homogeneous speech community. The people inside this polygon may have used several Turkic and Uralic varieties; no ninth-century language census survives.

Ancient DNA finds continuity among Uyelgi's chronological horizons and traces biological relationships across regions. Genes cannot tell us the name, language, loyalty, or bedtime stories of a person. Genetic affinity is valuable evidence about ancestry, and it remains a poor substitute for a self-declared ninth-century Bashkir identity.

Radiocarbon dates from six Uyelgi complexes span roughly 770 to 1020, with an early cluster from the late eighth through early tenth century and mainly in the ninth. This securely overlaps the card. A cemetery's use-life, however, does not establish the atlas label's start or end.

Kurgan 11 contains at least four cultural horizons. Its lower level follows Southern Ural nomadic practice, while upper burials include Srostki-related features, Altai-style belt fittings, and Ugric-associated pottery. Mixed objects document contact and changing practice more convincingly than a single ethnic sticker.

Uyelgi's ninth-, ninth-to-tenth-, and tenth-to-eleventh-century burial horizons show genetic continuity within a relatively endogamous group even while grave goods changed. That combination is a useful discovery: biological community and material fashion need not change together, and neither alone reveals a modern ethnic category.

Archaeologists report that a large majority of known Kushnarenkovo burials had been disturbed, and ancient looting also damaged Uyelgi graves. Missing objects and displaced bones complicate every reconstruction. A sparse grave may reflect robbery rather than poverty, simplicity, or a deliberate cultural rule.

Modern teams combine excavation plans, artifact typology, radiocarbon measurement, physical anthropology, and genetics. Each method answers a different question and carries uncertainty. Their achievement is not a perfect tribal map; it is a testable, revisable picture of communities whose own written explanations have not survived.

sections.title: Horses, belts, pottery, and skilled hands

items.text: Five Uyelgi and Sineglazovo burial complexes allow partial reconstruction of ninth- to eleventh-century Southern Trans-Ural equipment. Stirrups, bits, cheekpieces, buckles, plaques, and strap ends show careful leather-and-metal systems for riding. They document skilled craft and horse travel, not an all-purpose uniform worn by everyone.

One grave included separate horse remains and harness gear. Buried horses can express status, ritual, memory, and mobile life, but a cemetery cannot count every household's animals. The safe conclusion is that horses mattered deeply in some communities, not that every child owned a pony with matching silver tack.

Fragments of a clay vessel bear comb-and-cord decoration associated by the excavators with East Uralic and West Siberian Ugric traditions. A cooking or storage pot can travel, be copied, or cross family lines. Decoration maps relationships among crafts better than it maps a person's single identity.

Belts and harnesses combined iron working with cast or stamped decorative fittings. Their repeated pieces had to fit straps, bodies, and moving animals, so design was practical as well as showy. The archaeological achievement lies in coordinated materials and repairable systems, even when the makers remain unnamed.

Ancient robbers reached many graves before archaeologists did, which is a gloomy kind of proof that portable metalwork was valuable. Researchers reconstruct sets from what remains and from parallels elsewhere. A missing buckle may have been stolen, decayed, or never deposited, so certainty must stay proportional to the evidence.

A child's burial at Uyelgi contained a belt decorated with silver details. It is rare direct evidence that age and display could meet in burial. The belt cannot tell us the child's name, games, chores, parents, or cause of death, and burial clothing may differ from ordinary dress.

The cemetery contains people buried across several generations, but shared burial space does not automatically reveal nuclear families. Kinship can be investigated through DNA and grave arrangement; marriage rules, fosterage, adoption, affection, and household membership need different evidence. “Related” and “lived together” are not identical historical claims.

No reviewed source securely describes a ninth-century Bashkir wedding, inheritance rule, parenting custom, household size, or division of chores inside this polygon. Families certainly existed. Leaving the details open protects children and adults of the past from being dressed in customs recorded centuries later.

Ibn Fadlan's party included a Bashghird Muslim convert who served them and translated or mediated during the journey. One person demonstrates individual mobility and religious difference within a named population. He does not prove that his family, neighbors, or everyone in the atlas polygon shared one belief or occupation.

Children must have learned movement, speech, work, stories, and social expectations from older people, but no local lesson book or school list survives from 800 to 900. Archaeological objects show practiced skill, not the age or setting of instruction. The evidence supports learning without inventing a classroom.

The Southern Urals bring mountain taiga, mixed forest, open steppe edges, river valleys, lakes, caves, and karst close together. That ecological mosaic offered wood, pasture, fish, game, plants, water, and travel corridors. It also meant that daily work could differ sharply between nearby communities and seasons.

Horse gear and animal burial make riding and stock care visible, while pottery makes food handling visible only in outline. The excavated evidence does not provide a complete menu, recipe, dairy calendar, or famine diary. A pot proves somebody used a vessel; it does not reveal tonight's soup.

Volga Bulgar sites preserve imported objects and evidence for craft, agriculture, livestock, and long-distance routes reaching the Urals and Trans-Urals. Nearby exchange could move metal, ornaments, ideas, and people. It does not turn every artifact in the Bashkirs polygon into merchandise or identify who negotiated each trade.

Silver dirhams circulated as both valued metal and means of payment in changing Khazar and Bulgar-linked networks. A coin found far from its mint may have traveled hand to hand, as bullion, or inside a hoard. It is a travel witness with no surviving passenger list.

Wild-hive beekeeping is a celebrated long-lived tradition in present Bashkortostan, and UNESCO places deep roots in the region. It makes an excellent continuity clue, not a license to hand every ninth-century household a honey jar. Exact practitioners, techniques, and dates still require securely associated archaeological evidence.

Ibn Fadlan crossed territory he called Bashghird in 922, about twenty-two years after this card ends. A route reconstruction places the encounter around 3 May, shortly before the party reached the Volga Bulgars. His account is crucial near-context, but it cannot be silently moved backward into 800.

The 922 narrative reports a wooden object worn at the neck and explanations involving a supreme lord and subordinate lords connected with natural forces and human life. Scholars separate possible direct observation from information supplied through interpreters. Translation and the traveler's expectations shaped what reached the page.

Ibn Fadlan also records people who revered cranes, snakes, or fish, suggesting diversity within what he grouped under one name. These brief reports are not a complete theology and may contain misunderstanding. They matter most when kept plural, provisional, and later than the atlas interval.

The Bashghird Muslim convert traveling with the embassy warns against treating the group as religiously uniform. Individual conversion, service, and multilingual mediation could cross community lines. One convert neither makes the whole population Muslim nor leaves everyone else frozen in a single unchanging category of belief.

Ibn Fadlan uses frightening and insulting language about the people he met. That rhetoric belongs to an anxious outsider narrative and later acquired an influential afterlife. It should be studied as evidence about the observer and encounter, never recycled as a timeless personality test for Bashkirs.

Written-language sample for 800 to 900: none is securely attributable to Bashkir speech. No local inscription, letter, school text, or sentence can be quoted with responsible confidence. An empty sample is more informative than translating a modern Bashkir phrase backward across a millennium and calling it medieval.

Near-after external label: “باشغرد” (Bāshghird), the people-name as represented in medieval Arabic tradition. It is an Arabic outsider spelling associated with the 922 account, not a Bashkir-language sentence. The surviving textual witnesses are later copies, and scholarly editions record variant readings of foreign names.

Arabic letters had to approximate sounds in an unfamiliar name, while copyists could alter dots and readings. Forms such as Bāshghird, Bāshjird, or Bāshqird therefore require editorial judgment. A spelling variation may reflect script transmission rather than three different peoples or three certain pronunciations.

A substantial corpus that linguists can securely analyze as Bashkir-language writing belongs to the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and uses Arabic-based, Latin, and Cyrillic systems. That late record is valuable for language history. It cannot fill the ninth-century silence by itself.

Modern Bashkir is a living language with its own cataloged identity. Continuity matters, but modern vocabulary, spelling, and grammar should not be placed unchanged into mouths from 850. Historical communities may contribute to later identities without being miniature copies of their twenty-first-century descendants.

No reviewed excavation report identifies a securely ninth-century medicine kit, named healer, treatment manual, or diagnosis for the people under this atlas label. Graves document bodies and death more readily than nursing and recovery. The absence limits detail; it does not mean that families lacked practical care.

Most exact-period archaeology reviewed here comes from cemeteries, the wrong evidence class for reconstructing household toilets. No securely associated latrine, sewer, bathhouse, or waste rule is reported for this polygon in 800 to 900. Responsible history states that gap instead of inventing either spotless plumbing or comic filth.

Rivers, springs, lakes, and seasonal water shaped movement through the Southern Urals. Water availability is environmental context, not proof of drinking safety or a particular washing routine. People had to manage water and waste, but the reviewed evidence does not preserve their exact containers, rules, or distances.

Ancient DNA can reveal biological kinship and population continuity, while skeletal study may sometimes identify injury or disease. Neither automatically recovers remedies, bedside care, disability support, or childhood illness. A laboratory result can answer ancestry questions and still leave the human experience of sickness unknown.

The famous 922 description calls the Bashghird filthy, but it supplies no systematic sanitation survey and comes from a fearful outsider after this period. Repeating the insult as a toilet fact would be bad history and bad manners. Hygiene claims require facilities, residues, parasites, or careful comparative evidence.

sections.title: At 900 the color changes, people continue

items.text: At world-900 the Bashkirs feature is absent. Beloretsk, Sibay, Magnitogorsk, Chelyabinsk, and Orsk all switch to Oghuz Turks, while Ufa and Birsk remain Volga Bulgar. The complete repaint is exact atlas behavior, but the file contains no event record explaining a synchronized political takeover.

An Oghuz occupation of Pecheneg Volga-Ural lands is dated around 893-894, while the exact role of a Khazar alliance remains debated. That background makes regional change plausible, but it does not prove the website polygon was conquered whole or emptied in 900. Movement and a software seam are different questions.

By 1000 the same eastern and southern probes fall under the Kimek-Kipchak Khaganate, and by 1100 under the Cuman-Kipchak Confederation. These broad labels show successive atlas phases. They cannot be read as a four-frame animation in which every family instantly changes identity.

The modern Bashkir language and people are real continuities in the wider region, but continuity is made through change, mixture, memory, and later history. Respecting descendants does not require pretending that every ninth-century Trans-Ural burial already carried today's language, institutions, borders, and national name.

Uyelgi continued in use beyond 900, with later tenth- and eleventh-century horizons above or beside earlier burials. That archaeological continuity is a gentle final fact: the people who remembered and reused places did not consult the atlas before crossing its century line.

ending.text: The Bashkirs label ends at 900 only because the atlas repaints its eastern and southern footprint as Oghuz Turks. No reviewed source records a unified Bashkir state falling in that year. Late ninth-century steppe conflict and migration provide regional context without proving an exact conquest of this polygon. Modern Bashkir identity and language belong to a long later history that cannot be projected backward unchanged. The database therefore keeps fell null and names no single successor: the people, families, routes, and burial communities continued through a coarse editorial seam.
